topics.name: Greetings and social context
topics.description: Greetings depend on the language, the relationship between people and the situation. Learners can notice an example used by a speaker of the language they are studying.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2, 4, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: greetings and social context.
evidence: Identifies a context that may change the choice of greeting.
misconceptions: Every greeting is suitable in every situation.
topics.question: Why might you use a different greeting with a teacher and with a close friend?
topics.answer: The relationship and setting can affect the degree of formality and the words or signs used.
topics.explanation: A greeting carries social meaning as well as a literal message.
hints: Think about who is being greeted.
What might change in a formal setting?
topics.activity: Find two greetings in a trusted language-learning resource and discuss when a speaker might use each.

topics.name: Notice and reproduce language patterns
topics.description: Attending to sounds or, for signed languages, visual features can help learners recognise and reproduce familiar language accurately.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2, 4, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: notice and reproduce language patterns.
evidence: Notices and practises a specific feature of a familiar expression.
misconceptions: It is enough to copy only the broad shape of an unfamiliar word or sign.
topics.question: If you do not recognise part of a greeting, what can you do before trying it yourself?
topics.answer: Ask or look for a reliable model, observe it again and practise the part that was unclear.
topics.explanation: A clear model supports noticing the features that carry meaning.
hints: How can you see or hear the expression again?
Who or what could provide a reliable model?
topics.activity: Choose a short greeting from a trusted source, observe or listen twice, and practise it while checking the model.

topics.name: Introducing yourself in an additional language
topics.description: A short introduction uses a familiar pattern to share chosen information. A learner can use a fictional name and avoid sharing personal details.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2, 4, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: introducing yourself in an additional language.
evidence: Uses an appropriate familiar introduction pattern in a supported interaction.
misconceptions: An introduction activity requires sharing your real address or personal details.
topics.question: How can you practise introducing yourself without giving personal information?
topics.answer: Use a fictional name and a simple introduction pattern from the language being learned.
topics.explanation: The practice focuses on the language pattern without requiring private details.
hints: Could you make up a name?
Which short introduction have you learned?
topics.activity: Use a fictional character to practise a greeting and introduction with a trusted model.

topics.name: Names, identity and respectful communication
topics.description: Names and forms of address can carry cultural and personal meaning. People may have different preferences for how they are addressed.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2–4, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: names, identity and respectful communication.
evidence: Asks respectfully and uses the form of address the person chooses.
misconceptions: Everyone from a language community has the same naming preference.
topics.question: If you are unsure how someone prefers their name to be said, what is a respectful response?
topics.answer: Ask how they say it, listen or watch carefully, and practise using their preference.
topics.explanation: Asking gives the individual a chance to guide how their own name is used.
hints: Who is best placed to tell you their preference?
What could you do after asking?
topics.activity: Practise asking about a fictional name and repeat it carefully using a trusted speaker or signer as a model.

topics.name: Asking for clarification
topics.description: When a message is unclear, language learners can ask for repetition, slower communication or an explanation using a familiar phrase or sign.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2, 4, Novice 2 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: asking for clarification.
evidence: Uses a suitable clarification strategy during a supported exchange.
misconceptions: Asking for clarification means communication has failed.
topics.question: You miss a word in a conversation. What could you do to keep communicating?
topics.answer: Use a learned request for repetition or clarification, then listen or watch again.
topics.explanation: Clarification is a communication strategy that helps both people understand.
hints: You can ask for help.
Could the other person repeat or explain the message?
topics.activity: Practise a short exchange in which one person deliberately asks for a phrase to be repeated or explained.

topics.name: Expressing a preference
topics.description: Learners can use familiar vocabulary and a supported language pattern to say what they like or prefer in a familiar context.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2, 4, Novice 2 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: expressing a preference.
evidence: Uses a familiar expression to communicate a choice.
misconceptions: A vocabulary list by itself always communicates who likes what.
topics.question: How could you tell a partner which of two activities you prefer in the language you are learning?
topics.answer: Use a taught preference expression and name one of the activities; a gesture or visual support may also help.
topics.explanation: The message combines a preference pattern with a relevant word or sign.
hints: What phrase or sign means you like or prefer something?
Which activity are you choosing?
topics.activity: Choose two pictured activities and practise stating a preference, then ask a partner theirs.

topics.name: Family words and community variation
topics.description: Words for family and relationships can reflect social and cultural context. Families and language practices vary, so examples should not assume every family has the same structure.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2–4, Novice 2 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: family words and community variation.
evidence: Uses a respectful example and recognises that families and language use vary.
misconceptions: Every family uses the same relationships and terms.
topics.question: How can a classroom practise family vocabulary without assuming every learner has the same family?
topics.answer: Use a fictional family or let learners choose which relationships they want to describe.
topics.explanation: A fictional example supports language practice while respecting different circumstances.
hints: Must everyone describe their own family?
What could a fictional example include?
topics.activity: Use a fictional family diagram to practise chosen relationship words, following a reliable language resource.

topics.name: Choosing language for a relationship
topics.description: The words, signs or forms of address people choose may change with familiarity, age, role and situation; conventions differ among communities and individuals.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2–4, Novice 2 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: choosing language for a relationship.
evidence: Explains why audience and context matter when choosing a familiar expression.
misconceptions: A literal translation always communicates the same level of respect.
topics.question: Why should you check a greeting with a speaker or signer of the language?
topics.answer: They can explain how it is used in context and whether a different form would be appropriate.
topics.explanation: A direct word-for-word translation may miss social meaning.
hints: Who has knowledge of how the expression is used?
What information besides its literal meaning would help?
topics.activity: Compare a casual and a more formal model from the same language and discuss the contexts provided by the source.

topics.name: Connected descriptions
topics.description: As proficiency grows, learners can join familiar expressions to describe a person, place or routine in more than one connected sentence or sign sequence.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 4, Novice 3 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: connected descriptions.
evidence: Produces a short connected description using familiar structures.
misconceptions: A longer description is just unrelated words placed together.
topics.question: How could you extend “The park is large” into a short description?
topics.answer: Add a relevant detail using a taught structure, such as what people can do there.
topics.explanation: A second related detail develops the same topic.
hints: What else could someone learn about the park?
Use a connection you have already practised.
topics.activity: Using a picture of a fictional place, compose two related statements in the language being learned and check them with a model.

topics.name: Talking about events in time
topics.description: Languages express time in different ways. A learner can use a taught time expression or grammatical pattern to make clear when a familiar event occurs.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 4, Novice 3 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: talking about events in time.
evidence: Communicates the time of a familiar event using a taught pattern.
misconceptions: Every language marks past and future in the same grammatical way as English.
topics.question: Why might “yesterday” and “tomorrow” change the meaning of the same activity?
topics.answer: They place the activity at different times, so the listener understands whether it has already happened or is expected later.
topics.explanation: Time information helps a listener place an event accurately.
hints: Which word refers to a past day?
Which refers to a future day?
topics.activity: Place three event cards in past, present and future groups; practise a taught time expression for each in the target language.

topics.name: Perspectives within a language community
topics.description: A language community contains people with varied experiences, regional practices and preferences. Reliable sources and community voices help learners understand context.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 3–4, Novice 3 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: perspectives within a language community.
evidence: Describes a perspective without treating it as universal.
misconceptions: One example represents every member of a community.
topics.question: A source describes one community custom. Can you assume everyone in that community follows it?
topics.answer: No. Ask whose perspective the source presents and look for other relevant voices and local context.
topics.explanation: One account can be useful without representing everyone.
hints: Who is speaking in the source?
Could people have different experiences?
topics.activity: Compare two attributed accounts from speakers or signers about a shared situation and note one similarity and one difference.

topics.name: Planning an interaction for an audience
topics.description: Planning an exchange involves choosing appropriate language and communication supports for the people and situation involved.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 2, 4, Novice 3 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: planning an interaction for an audience.
evidence: Plans an interaction that considers the listener and situation.
misconceptions: An interaction only needs correct vocabulary; the listener and setting do not matter.
topics.question: You are preparing to ask for information at a community event. What should you consider?
topics.answer: Consider a suitable greeting, a clear question, a way to clarify the response and the audience's communication needs.
topics.explanation: Preparation combines language knowledge with attention to the context and the other person.
hints: How will you begin politely?
What could you do if the answer is unclear?
topics.activity: Role-play a fictional enquiry using a greeting, one question and a clarification strategy from a trusted model.

topics.name: Te reo Māori: greeting in context
topics.description: Kia ora can be used in several everyday contexts, including greeting and thanks. Other greetings and farewells suit different people and situations.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 8, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: te reo māori: greeting in context.
evidence: Recognises at least two contexts for a familiar te reo Māori greeting.
misconceptions: A familiar greeting can only have one use in every context.
topics.question: What can “kia ora” communicate in an everyday interaction?
topics.answer: It can be used as a greeting or to express thanks, depending on context.
topics.explanation: The intended meaning is informed by the situation and relationship.
hints: The phrase can have more than one everyday use.
Think about meeting someone and receiving help.
topics.activity: Listen to an attributed te reo Māori speaker using a greeting, then practise it in two short fictional situations.

topics.name: Te reo Māori: vowel length and macrons
topics.description: A macron marks a long vowel in written te reo Māori, and vowel length can distinguish words. Pronunciation should be learned from reliable speakers, with attention to regional variation.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 8, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: te reo māori: vowel length and macrons.
evidence: Recognises a macron and describes its role in vowel length.
misconceptions: Macrons are decorative marks with no effect on meaning.
topics.question: What does the macron show in a written Māori vowel?
topics.answer: It marks a long vowel.
topics.explanation: The mark carries pronunciation information and can distinguish meanings.
hints: Look at the line above the vowel.
It signals a difference in vowel length.
topics.activity: Use a trusted audio model to compare a short and a long vowel; mark the long vowel in a copied example.

topics.name: Te reo Māori: names and address
topics.description: Te reo Māori greetings can include names and terms of address. Usage is shaped by language knowledge and the situation.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 12, Novice 2 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: te reo māori: names and address.
evidence: Considers a person's preference when choosing a form of address.
misconceptions: All terms of address can be exchanged without changing meaning.
topics.question: What should you do if you are unsure of the appropriate name or term of address?
topics.answer: Ask the person or a trusted speaker and follow their guidance.
topics.explanation: The choice of address can carry social meaning and should respect the person's preference.
hints: Whose preference matters?
Who can explain the language form in context?
topics.activity: Practise a greeting with a fictional name, then compare it with an attributed language example.

topics.name: Te reo Māori: connections to place
topics.description: A mihi may acknowledge connections to people and place. The details and appropriate practices depend on the speaker and local context; learners should use guidance from the relevant community.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 14, Novice 3 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: te reo māori: connections to place.
evidence: Identifies the value of local guidance and avoids inventing personal or community connections.
misconceptions: A single template can accurately supply anyone's whakapapa or local tikanga.
topics.question: Why should a learner seek local guidance before using a place-based introduction?
topics.answer: Local communities and speakers can explain appropriate names, relationships and practices for that context.
topics.explanation: Connections to place and their expression can be specific to people and communities.
hints: Who holds knowledge about the place?
Could practices differ between communities?
topics.activity: Examine an attributed public example of a mihi and identify how the speaker acknowledges place; do not invent another person's connections.

topics.name: Mandarin: pinyin and tone
topics.description: Pinyin represents Mandarin pronunciation with Roman letters and tone marks. Tone can distinguish the meanings of otherwise similar syllables.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 8, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: mandarin: pinyin and tone.
evidence: Recognises that a pinyin tone mark represents pronunciation information.
misconceptions: Tone marks are optional decoration with no role in meaning.
topics.question: What additional information does a tone mark give in pinyin?
topics.answer: It indicates the tone of the syllable.
topics.explanation: Tone is part of pronunciation and can affect meaning.
hints: Look at the mark above the vowel.
Does it tell you about the pitch pattern?
topics.activity: Listen to a trusted recording of two familiar syllables with different tones and match them to the written pinyin.

topics.name: Mandarin: characters and components
topics.description: Chinese characters are written forms that can contain recurring components. Words may contain one or more characters; simplified and traditional forms are used in different communities.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 8–9, Novice 1 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: mandarin: characters and components.
evidence: Distinguishes a character from a word using a familiar example.
misconceptions: Every Chinese character is a complete word and every word has one character.
topics.question: Does every Chinese word have to contain exactly one character?
topics.answer: No. Chinese words can contain one or more characters.
topics.explanation: A character and a word are different units, even when one character forms a word.
hints: Compare a one-character word with a two-character word.
Count the characters in each.
topics.activity: Choose a familiar two-character word from a reliable dictionary, count its characters and discuss their contribution to the word.

topics.name: Mandarin: greetings and formality
topics.description: Mandarin greetings include forms used in different relationships and situations; respectful choices can depend on the person being addressed.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 9, 12, Novice 2 (proficiency-based); Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: mandarin: greetings and formality.
evidence: Distinguishes a familiar casual greeting from a more polite one.
misconceptions: A greeting has the same social meaning regardless of form or audience.
topics.question: Why might a learner choose 您好 rather than 你好 in a formal exchange?
topics.answer: 您好 is a polite form that can be appropriate in a respectful or formal setting.
topics.explanation: The choice of pronoun helps signal the relationship and formality.
hints: Compare 你 and 您 in a trusted resource.
Which form is typically more polite?
topics.activity: Practise two fictional greetings, one casual and one more formal, and explain why the choices differ.

topics.name: Mandarin: expressing an opinion
topics.description: A learner can express a simple opinion in Mandarin and add a reason using language structures they have already practised.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 18, Novice 3 (proficiency-based); Linguistic Knowledge
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: mandarin: expressing an opinion.
evidence: Expresses a simple opinion with a relevant reason using familiar structures.
misconceptions: An opinion and a supporting reason do exactly the same job.
topics.question: What makes an opinion more informative than naming a preference alone?
topics.answer: It can include a reason or detail explaining the preference.
topics.explanation: A reason helps the listener understand the speaker's thinking.
hints: What do you think?
Why do you think it?
topics.activity: Use a fictional choice between two activities and practise a short opinion plus a reason with an appropriate language model.

topics.name: NZSL: four features of a sign
topics.description: A sign can be described through its handshape, orientation, location and movement. Learners should watch a reliable Deaf language model to see how these work together.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Novice 1 > Linguistic Knowledge: formational parameters
objectives: Watch a teacher-approved NZSL model and note the four features of one demonstrated sign without guessing its meaning.
evidence: Identifies the four sign features in a model.
misconceptions: Only handshape matters in a signed language.
topics.question: Which four features help describe the form of an NZSL sign?
topics.answer: Handshape, orientation, location and movement.
topics.explanation: A sign can be described through its handshape, orientation, location and movement. Learners should watch a reliable Deaf language model to see how these work together.
hints: Consider both the hand and where it is used.
How is the hand shaped and facing, and where and how does it move?
topics.activity: Watch a teacher-approved NZSL model and note the four features of one demonstrated sign without guessing its meaning.

topics.name: NZSL: visual attention and access
topics.description: NZSL communication needs a clear view of the signer’s face, hands and body. Gaining attention respectfully helps make a visual conversation accessible.
topics.locator: PDF p. 10, Novice 1 > Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge: visual attention and gaining attention; line of sight also supported by official overview glossary
objectives: Arrange two seats for clear sightlines and explain how each person can see the other’s face and hands.
evidence: Explains how the arrangement supports a visual conversation.
misconceptions: A signer’s hands are the only part a viewer needs to see.
topics.question: Why should two signers maintain a clear line of sight?
topics.answer: So each can see the signs and facial or body cues that carry meaning.
topics.explanation: NZSL communication needs a clear view of the signer’s face, hands and body. Gaining attention respectfully helps make a visual conversation accessible.
hints: How is the message received?
What happens if the signer’s face or hands are hidden?
topics.activity: Arrange two seats for clear sightlines and explain how each person can see the other’s face and hands.

topics.name: NZSL: facial and body signals
topics.description: Facial expressions and body movements can contribute grammatical information to NZSL. Their meaning must be learned from an authentic model in context.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 13, 15, Novice 2 > Linguistic Knowledge: non-manual signals and facial grammar
objectives: Watch a teacher-selected Deaf signer and note the visible facial and body signals alongside hand movement.
evidence: Observes non-manual signals without inventing a translation.
misconceptions: Facial expression is always decorative and carries no linguistic information.
topics.question: Why should a viewer watch a signer’s face as well as their hands?
topics.answer: Facial and other non-manual signals can contribute to the signed message and its grammar.
topics.explanation: Facial expressions and body movements can contribute grammatical information to NZSL. Their meaning must be learned from an authentic model in context.
hints: Where else can grammatical information appear?
Think about the signer’s face and body.
topics.activity: Watch a teacher-selected Deaf signer and note the visible facial and body signals alongside hand movement.

topics.name: NZSL: name signs and community
topics.description: A name sign is given by a Deaf person; the curriculum glossary cautions against giving yourself one or a hearing person assigning one.
topics.locator: PDF p. 13, Novice 2 > Linguistic Knowledge: name signs given by Deaf community; official overview glossary: appropriate name-sign practice
objectives: Discuss a fictional introduction and identify who could offer guidance on a name sign; do not invent one.
evidence: Explains why the learner should seek guidance from a Deaf person.
misconceptions: Anyone should invent their own NZSL name sign.
topics.question: Who should a learner look to for an appropriate NZSL name sign?
topics.answer: A Deaf person, rather than inventing or assigning one themselves.
topics.explanation: A name sign is given by a Deaf person; the curriculum glossary cautions against giving yourself one or a hearing person assigning one.
hints: Who has knowledge of the language community?
Does choosing your own name sign respect that practice?
topics.activity: Discuss a fictional introduction and identify who could offer guidance on a name sign; do not invent one.

topics.name: NZSL: using signing space
topics.description: NZSL uses locations in signing space to connect people, objects or ideas and show relationships among them.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Novice 3 > Linguistic Knowledge: spatial referencing
objectives: Watch a teacher-selected signed story and sketch the locations the signer uses for two characters.
evidence: Identifies two referents and the locations used to distinguish them.
misconceptions: Signing space has no role in conveying relationships.
topics.question: What can spatial referencing help a signer show?
topics.answer: Relationships between people, objects or ideas by assigning and using locations in signing space.
topics.explanation: NZSL uses locations in signing space to connect people, objects or ideas and show relationships among them.
hints: How might space organise people in a story?
Can locations help the viewer keep track of referents?
topics.activity: Watch a teacher-selected signed story and sketch the locations the signer uses for two characters.

topics.name: Gagana Sāmoa: hearing a glottal stop
topics.description: A glottal stop is a brief interruption of airflow. Listen to a fluent speaker or trusted audio to hear how it occurs in the language.
topics.locator: PDF p. 8, Novice 1 > Linguistic Knowledge: glottal stop
objectives: Listen to a teacher-approved Gagana Sāmoa recording and mark where the model includes a brief sound break.
evidence: Identifies a short interruption in the supplied recording.
misconceptions: Every sound in a word must be continuous.
topics.question: What is a glottal stop?
topics.answer: A brief closure and release of the vocal folds that interrupts the airflow.
topics.explanation: A glottal stop is a brief interruption of airflow. Listen to a fluent speaker or trusted audio to hear how it occurs in the language.
hints: Does the voice continue without interruption?
What brief closure can create a catch in the sound?
topics.activity: Listen to a teacher-approved Gagana Sāmoa recording and mark where the model includes a brief sound break.

topics.name: Gagana Sāmoa: language and setting
topics.description: The form of language can vary with the occasion. Ceremonial language is associated with formal cultural events; community guidance matters for a particular setting.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 11–12, Novice 2 > Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge: formal and cultural contexts; overview glossary: ceremonial language
objectives: Compare a teacher-provided classroom introduction and a description of a formal occasion, without performing ceremonial speech.
evidence: Identifies the different settings and seeks community guidance for the formal example.
misconceptions: One expression is automatically appropriate for every event.
topics.question: Why might a classroom greeting differ from language used at a formal event?
topics.answer: The occasion and participants can call for a different level or form of language.
topics.explanation: The form of language can vary with the occasion. Ceremonial language is associated with formal cultural events; community guidance matters for a particular setting.
hints: Who is present at each event?
How does the formality of the situation change?
topics.activity: Compare a teacher-provided classroom introduction and a description of a formal occasion, without performing ceremonial speech.

topics.name: Gagana Tokelau: noticing intonation
topics.description: Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement across an utterance and can contribute to communicative meaning. A speaker model helps learners notice the pattern.
topics.locator: PDF p. 8, Novice 1 > Cultural and Sociolinguistic Knowledge: intonation; p. 7 Novice 1 listening and speaking practice
objectives: Listen to two teacher-selected Gagana Tokelau recordings and sketch arrows for the pitch movement.
evidence: Identifies an upward or downward pitch pattern in a model.
misconceptions: Intonation only means speaking more loudly.
topics.question: What changes when a speaker uses rising intonation?
topics.answer: The pitch rises across the relevant part of the utterance.
topics.explanation: Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement across an utterance and can contribute to communicative meaning. A speaker model helps learners notice the pattern.
hints: Listen for the pitch rather than the loudness.
Does the pitch travel upward or downward?
topics.activity: Listen to two teacher-selected Gagana Tokelau recordings and sketch arrows for the pitch movement.

topics.name: Gagana Tokelau: language across generations
topics.description: Language, skills and stories may be shared across generations. Individuals choose what they are comfortable sharing and different families have different experiences.
topics.locator: Official Gagana Tokelau overview glossary: intergenerational knowledge; Novice 2 editorial placement, not yet checked against the language-specific teaching sequence
objectives: Prepare a voluntary, non-personal question for a language speaker and practise thanking them for any response.
evidence: Asks a respectful question without assuming anyone must share family information.
misconceptions: Every family has the same story and must share it.
topics.question: How could a learner respectfully learn about language used across generations?
topics.answer: Ask an appropriate speaker whether they wish to share and follow their guidance.
topics.explanation: Language, skills and stories may be shared across generations. Individuals choose what they are comfortable sharing and different families have different experiences.
hints: Who has knowledge of the language?
Should sharing be voluntary?
